en: The Record of the Lotus Sutra,
Volume One I pay homage to the Great Teacher of Gods and Humans, To Śākyamuni, the Honored One, whose three bodies are one essence,
The Lord who appears in the world within the gateway of the five Buddhas of the three periods And expounds the One Vehicle.
I pay homage to the Dharma Flower Sūtra, To the Buddha Prabhūtaratna who testifies to it, And to all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions who manifest their bodies,
Extending even to the ocean of the entire dharma-realm of empty space,
To the World-Hero who abides eternally and his manifested bodies, And to the eighty-one thousand holy teachings.
The great treasure-store protected by all Buddhas, The immeasurable and unfathomable scripture of benefit and bliss—
I take refuge in Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and the rest, The eighty thousand Great Beings, the Dharma-Prince sons of the Buddha,
The thousands of world-realms of *sattvas* who have emerged from the earth, And the eighty trillion *nayutas* of them.
The Bodhisattvas such as Gadgadasvara, Avalokiteśvara, and Samantabhadra, who have made vows to propagate this sutra;
their five eyes are fully perfected and they illuminate the world, universally manifesting physical forms to appear identical with the mundane dust.
Śāriputra, Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, and others—these tens of billions of śrāvakas are true sons of the Buddha.
From our own realm and other directions, immeasurable beings—whether taught through provisional or ultimate means—all who are to be transformed;

I have compiled these scriptures to protect the city of the Dharma. Out of compassion, may you shield and protect us, and grant us your majestic power, so that the lamp of the Dharma shall not be extinguished but shine long through the night, and by this, those who are deluded may attain the wisdom of a Buddha.

In the age of the final dharma, those who hear the Lotus Sūtra even once and rejoice in it will have all their karmic obstacles of the three periods of time completely extinguished; within three lifetimes, they shall certainly enter the stage of right determination.
May the wondrous Dharma long abide in the world, circulating throughout all lands in the ten directions.
All who encounter this together give rise to joy; throughout every lifetime they shall constantly hear it and be able to practice it.
Even those who see, hear, praise, or revile it—whether their conditions be favorable or adverse—all shall realize the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Whether spoken with harsh words or gentle speech, they all return to a single meaning, never contradicting one another until reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Furthermore, the wondrous causes nurtured by Xiang over many lifetimes have now manifested:
he has propagated the One Vehicle and extolled the sublime texts.
With my eyes I heard what had never been heard before;
with my ears I saw what had never been seen before.
Long ago, during the Yao Qin dynasty, I first sought the Way.
As for the benefit of its circulation during the reign of our Great Tang, which has possessed the empire,
there was nothing like it in previous dynasties.
The resonance of spiritual response is without premeditation; it cannot be fathomed by calculation.
Its wondrous benefits are concentrated and profound.
This is also what has been verified by the measuring cord of the scriptures.
Now, I have briefly compiled what I have seen and heard with my own ears and eyes,
in order to inspire the faith of future generations.
These are categorized into twelve sections and divided into ten fascicles:
the categories of hidden and manifest, translated and transmitted lineages, sutras, prefaces, commentaries, exegeses, recitation, chanting, transcription, listening, and making offerings.
I have briefly cited three or five examples from each,
compiling their topical outlines;
the language is plain and colloquial.
I desire that those who see and hear this may easily attain awakening;
by making the essential points clear and substantial,
I shall ensure the transmission of faith to future generations.
Furthermore, I have further explored and obtained various records, commentaries, and biographies composed by the different schools, both ancient and new;
these I have transcribed and extracted here. Should anything more be acquired in the future, it shall likewise be recorded.
I also wish to follow [the tradition] and compile it;
should the compilation be lost, may future readers arrange it in order,
thereby causing the sublime Dharma and its true texts to flourish once more.
The vehicles of the teachings are inexhaustible;
first the table of contents is set forth,
and thereafter they are collected accordingly.

Chapter Three: The Dates of Translation; Chapter Five: Differences in Exegesis; Chapter Seven: Explaining Resonance and Response; Chapter Nine: Eradicating Sin through Recitation; Chapter Eleven: Benefits of Hearing [the Dharma]. Section One: The Increase and Decrease of Scriptural Categories. Regarding the increase and decrease of scriptural categories: first, as for the term "increase and decrease of scriptural categories."
The capacities and inclinations [of sentient beings] vary between extensive and concise,
which consequently results in an increase or decrease in the number of categories. Although there is such increase or decrease, [the essence remains the same].
Without losing their implicit or explicit benefits,
these are briefly categorized into seven examples.
First, the sūtras of a single assembly are treated as a single collection.
First, those such as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
where [the teachings] are arranged according to stages; second, those such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, where many assemblies are compiled together into a single work.
Third, those where the initial portion of a sūtra constitutes a single work,
such as the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.
Fourth, those where both portions are complete and constitute a single work.
Such as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and others.
Fifth, condensing the original text into a single volume,
such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (Small Version Sūtra) and others.
Sixth, expanding a single broad version to constitute one entire collection,
as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others.
Seventh, treating a single chapter as one entire collection.
As in the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra,
so too in this Lotus Sūtra,
it contains the complete original version.
If one follows the Sanskrit manuscript,
the text should be an abbreviated explanation. Why is this so?
This sutra is a teaching on the quiescence of subject and object, wherein the three bodies are of one essence.
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni Buddha..."
He is named Vairocana, pervading all places.
The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constantly Quiescent Light,
established by the four pāramitās.
The Dharma King, having opened the auspicious fortune and finished preaching the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*,
entered the meditative concentration on the locus of meaning.
He manifested extraordinary and auspicious omens to inspire profound reverence in the great assembly,
together with eighty thousand great bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī.
Śāriputra and ten trillion other great śrāvakas, the eight nāgas,
the four kinnaras, the four gandharvas, and so forth,
as well as those of the six heavens and the four dhyānas.
Ten trillion wheel-turning sage-kings,
kings, princes, princesses, and commoners—
an assembly of inconceivable, unspeakably many oceans of followers.
This is what was taught:
beginning thus and concluding with "departing."
All are the wondrous Dharma;
every syllable is bound in wonder.
Not a single character or phrase is not the Dharma-realm.
Every single character and every single dot is none other than the Buddha.
Above, they exhaustively encompass the meritorious virtues of Vairocana;
below, they reach down to the environment and its inhabitants of the Avīci Hell.
Neither identical nor separate,
its essence is endowed with the subtle and inconceivable;
this is the perfect *sūtra*, the nectar-like jewel of the Dharma.
According to tradition in the West,
the text compiled during the eight-year assembly on Vulture Peak should have covered an area of one yojana.
If one were to compile them all,
there would be no place to contain the assembly of immeasurable and boundless beings gathered like the ocean.
It causes them to attain understanding.

It consists of the correct exposition, the comprehension and realization, the summary and confirmation, the bestowal of prophecy, the joyful recitation of verses, and the praise of the Buddha and the making of vows by those in one's own realm and other realms;
each chapter is accomplished through immeasurable and boundless words and meanings.
Just as the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū spoke this Lotus Sutra in verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The Buddha Prabhūtaratna spoke the verses beginning with "Kañcana, Piṅgala, Akṣobhya," and so forth;
[and] King Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.
He spoke twenty thousand *koṭis* of verses;
the present Buddha is likewise.
*Puṇḍarīka* is also said to have spoken countless verses.
At that time, a stupa made of the seven precious jewels suddenly appeared before him. Once the jeweled stupa had appeared, [he said:
"The jeweled stupa has already appeared."
There were incalculable verses,
and furthermore, a multitude emerged,
praising with various dharmas of the bodhisattvas.
And they praised the Buddha with various verses of praise as numerous as the atoms within a thousand worlds;
who could know the number of those verses?
The Tripitaka Master Jue’ai said:
According to tradition in the West,
when the Buddha preached the Lotus Sūtra, [he performed this mudrā].
It cannot be fully described; within each chapter,
there are many verses and phrases.
Using Mount Sumeru as a bundle of brushes and the great ocean as ink and water,
one would write down every single chapter and every single verse.
It is inexhaustible.
The Buddha always dwells on Mount Ling,
together with the great bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
He preached the Dharma while surrounded by a vast assembly;
gods and humans filled the space from the beginningless past to the endless future.
It continues without rest;
it is sustained solely by the power of the inexhaustible dhāraṇī,
and cannot be recorded by means of brush or ink.
However, based on the karmic responses of beings during a single period,
[the teachings] were compiled into one collection over eight years; thus,
although it was a brief compilation, it was completed.
The leaves spread over an area of one yojana;
according to the most concise version of the original text,
they fill a room of ten feet square.
The general outline of the twenty-eight chapters is complete.
Furthermore, as the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated,
the records of the Western Regions say:
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna traveled by sea to the Dragon Palace,
where he beheld this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samapramāda-mahāyāna-sūtra*,
consisting of verses as numerous as the atoms of a great trichiliocosm and chapters as numerous as the dust motes of the four continents.
It fully records the successive layers of questions and answers regarding the wondrous omens,
as manifested within the light appearing in the eastern lands, the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below; furthermore,
there were twenty billion lamps of illumination.
In each instance, he preached the ritual of the Lotus Sūtra,
extolling the great causal conditions for the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time,
thereby transforming those of the three vehicles.
The realization of the One Vehicle;

the Buddhas’ bestowal of predictions upon Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas based on their original conditions; the Buddha’s own discourse on the inexhaustible, layered, and ineffable succession of his own joints; the making of vows to propagate and uphold [the Dharma] in one's own realm and other directions; the emergence of verses of praise; and the expedient means following the fruition, such as the assemblies gathering from the ten directions—these and other matters.
This is exactly as described in the section on "Hidden and Manifest.
Currently, four different versions are transmitted in Chang’an:
the first consists of five thousand stanzas.
The one transmitted by Zheng Wuweai is this [version].
The one translated by Zhu Fahu consists of twenty-six thousand five hundred verses. This is that [version].
Three thousand six hundred verses;
this is the version transmitted by Kumārajīva.
Four thousand two hundred verses.
That which was transmitted by Jñānagupta is this [version].
The three editions were written on *tāla* leaves;
the version of Kumārajīva was written on white cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
Regarding what has been transmitted in this land,
there are still variations in the number of verses;
as for the extent of the sūtras in the Western Regions, how can they be measured?
However, according to tradition,
the Sanskrit text consists of only twenty-eight chapters,
and none of them have titles preceding the text.
It is simply called Siddham;
this is translated as "Auspicious Dharma" (Kikyōhō) and is also named "Accomplishment" (Jōju).
The names [of these sections] are not established;
they all appear at the end of the chapter or at the conclusion of the sutra,
yet those that originally followed have been moved to the beginning.
It is likely that the translators,
following the conventions of the land of China,
intended to distinguish the various classes [of texts] based on differences in terminology.
However, the twenty-seven chapters of the many extant manuscripts merely conclude with the title "Knotting the End," omitting the chapter on Deva.
Matters that differ are as follows in the translated transmission:
some divide the chapters into sections.
As distinguished by the following branches: the expansion or brevity depends on the capacity [of the recipient],
while the categories may increase or decrease.

The Difference Between the Times of Concealment and Manifestation. Second, according to the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*:
Four hundred and fifty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
Mañjuśrī was still present in the world.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
The various Mahāyāna sūtras were compiled by Mañjuśrī,
according to the tradition of the transmission of the Dharma collection.
There are three kinds of Ānanda;
"Ānanda" is translated here as "Joy.
He is the holder of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
Ānandabhadra means "Joyful Sage" (Huanxi Xian) in Chinese;
he maintains the treasury of the pratyekabuddhas.
Ānandakara means "Ocean of Joy" (Huanxi Hai) in Chinese.
When Ānanda ascended the high seat, sentient beings harbored three doubts:
first, they doubted that the Buddha’s great compassion had arisen from nirvāṇa to preach the wondrous Dharma;
second, they doubted that another Buddha had come from another direction to dwell here and preach the Dharma.
Third, [he addressed] those who doubted that Ānanda had transformed his body to become a Buddha and was preaching the Dharma for the assembly.
He now reveals that the Dharma thus preached is that which he himself formerly attended to while serving the Buddha.
Regarding the fact that he personally heard [the teaching] twenty-five years ago:
it was not the case that the Buddha had already departed for another realm and a different Buddha arrived to manifest as the Buddha;
rather, this was taught in order to eliminate such doubts.
At the beginning of all sūtras, it is said, "Thus have I heard.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that this is clarified in the *Vinaya-sūkṣma*.
When Ānanda ascended to a high place to compile the Dharma-piṭaka,
his body was like that of the Buddhas,
endowed with all the primary and secondary marks of excellence.
When descending from his seat,
he returns to his original form;
this is truly because his provisional practice is fully endowed with the three virtues.
Both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions transmit this;
this sutra was compiled by Ānanda Sāgara. If it is a discourse spoken by the Buddha, [it must be accepted].
Mañjuśrī was seated in the assembly and first proclaimed the titles of the sūtras;
Ānanda ascended to a high place and recited them again for compilation.
Based on this, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Mañjuśrī compiled all the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Having completed the compilation,
they immediately inscribed it upon *vinyasa* leaves and deposited them within the Ratnapatra Cave.
The great assembly of devas, humans, nāgas, rājās,
and ministers vied with one another to present offerings.
After the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, [the stupa] remained.
The worthy sages followed into seclusion,
just as a great elephant follows its calf when it departs. Then,
the ninety-five heterodox paths arose in chaotic confusion.
Eighteen heterodox teachers exclusively venerated the Hinayana scriptures;
consequently, most Mahayana sutras were obscured and did not circulate in the world.
After this sūtra had been compiled,
it was concealed and not practiced;
thus it has been transmitted in the West.
Within the Great Snow Mountains there is a jeweled stupa that preserves the Sanskrit manuscripts of the Lotus Sūtra,
exactly as described by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha.
According to the records of the Western Regions,
at the end of the fifth century after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was a bhikṣu.
He profoundly understood the Mahāyāna,
attained the realization of non-arising,
and sought out profound sūtras everywhere.
He traveled to the Snowy Mountains,
where he opened the doors of the precious stupa and unrolled the Sanskrit scriptures for examination.
Dwelling therein, he guarded and upheld it.
At the beginning of the sixth hundred years,
there was a member of the brahmin caste in the land of South India.
He thoroughly mastered the great meanings of the four Vedas, the five sciences, and the eighteen heterodox scriptures;
his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias, and he walked alone as the peerless master among all nations.
He was named Nāgārjuna.
He abandoned heterodoxy to return to the orthodox path and left the household life to receive the precepts.
For ninety days, he deliberated on and recited the Tripiṭaka; yet, though he sought the profound Dharma, he found no place where it could be attained.
He then entered a stūpa in the Snow Mountains and bestowed this Sanskrit manuscript of the sūtra upon Nāgārjuna, who received it,
recited it, and took great delight in it.
Not yet knowing the true meaning,
he traveled through various countries to seek out other sutras,
searching throughout Jambudvīpa.
Unable to obtain it in its entirety,
he remained alone in a quiet chamber within a crystal pavilion, contemplating this matter.
The Dragon King of the Great Ocean saw him and took pity on him;
he drew forth eight great oceans from within his palace and produced a casket of the seven treasures.

He bestowed upon him the Avataṃsaka, the Lotus, the various Mahāyāna Cloud Sūtras, the Great Cloud, the Flower-Hand, the Pratyutpanna, and other profound Vaipulya sūtras of immeasurable wondrous Dharma.
Nāgārjuna received and recited [the teachings] for ninety days;
his mind entered deeply into them, and he personally realized their true benefit.
The Naga King, knowing his state of mind, asked:
[The questioner] said, "I have not yet finished reading the scriptures. He replied,
"The scriptures within your various cases are immeasurably numerous."
It could not be exhausted even in an eon.
What I have read and mastered already exceeds ten times the extent of the sutras of Jambudvīpa.
The Dragon King said,
"As for all the scriptures within my palace,
those in other places comparable to them are beyond counting."
Each and every one is as numerous as motes of dust, yet they do not obstruct or hinder one another;
this is inconceivable. Nāgārjuna said:
"I pray that you may obtain the profound sutras and return to Jambudvīpa to extensively propagate the Buddha-dharma and subdue the non-Buddhists.
The Dragon King said:
In my palace, there are three versions of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* of inconceivable liberation.
The superior version contains verses as numerous as the atoms in thirteen worlds and chapters as numerous as the atoms in the four continents.
The middle version consists of four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters;
the abbreviated version consists of one hundred thousand stanzas and thirty chapters.
This is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samavasaraṇa-sūtra*.
There are chapters on the Ineffable containing as many verses as there are atoms in ten worlds;
other scriptures are exceedingly vast and extensive.
Nāgārjuna said:
"I see that this wondrous scripture is inconceivable;
how shall it be transmitted?
The Dragon King said:
The two versions of the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*, the upper and middle fascicles,
have reached a point where they cannot be received or upheld by the power of human beings in Jambudvīpa;
they must not be transmitted.
The abbreviated version of the profound Lotus Sutra remains in Jambudvīpa;
the extensive versions are all kept secret within my palace.
He immediately bestowed upon him a chest containing the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* in its shorter version as well as various other sūtras.
Once Nāgārjuna had obtained this chest, he entered deeply into the realization of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Nāgārjuna traveled south to South India,
where he greatly propagated the Buddha's teachings and subdued the non-Buddhists.
He extensively expounded the Mahāyāna,
composing three great treatises and one thousand individual commentaries;
within these great treatises, he frequently cited the Avataṃsaka, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, and other sutras.
The commentary on the profound and subtle meaning states at length:
"If one follows this biographical record,
since there already exists a major version [of the text]..."
It was kept secret within the Dragon Palace and remained hidden,
not being transmitted. The *Xiyu zhi* (Record of the Western Regions) states:
Formerly, there was a Sanskrit manuscript of the Lotus Sūtra in the royal palace of Khotan,
consisting of six thousand five hundred verses.
It is located more than two thousand li to the southeast.
There was a kingdom named Cīnapaṭṭana.
For generations, its kings had revered the Mahāyāna;
whenever monks renowned throughout various lands entered its borders, they were received with honor.
He tested their understanding in all cases;
those who studied the Hīnayāna were dismissed without being retained,
while those of the Mahāyāna were invited to receive exquisite offerings.
The royal palace also possessed five great sūtras— the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*—
each consisting of one hundred thousand verses,
which the King personally received and upheld.
The master personally took hold of the door-bolt;
when the recitation began, it opened.
He then made offerings of incense and flowers.
Furthermore, more than twenty li to the southeast,
there is a mountain that is extremely steep and difficult to traverse; upon its peak is a stone cave.
Deceptive in speech yet broad within,

he internally upholds the Avataṃsaka, Mahāsaṃnipāta, Vaipulya, Ratnakūṭa, Laṅkāvatāra, Vaipulya, Śāriputra-dhāraṇī, Puṣpakūṭa-dhāraṇī, Tausara, Mahāprajñāpāramitā, Mahāmegha, and Saddharmapuṇḍarīka sūtras.
There are twelve divisions in total,
each consisting of one hundred thousand verses;
according to the laws of the kingdom, these have been handed down through tradition and are carefully guarded and preserved.
It is further stated:
"In the palace of the King of Kaśmīra, there is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consisting of six thousand verses," and so forth.
Inferring from the time he was active in this world,
it corresponds to the forty-fifth year, *Yichou*, through the fifty-second year, *Renshen*, of King Mu of Zhou in this land.
Having finished speaking, he entered nirvana.
For more than a thousand years after his parinirvāṇa,
[this teaching] was neither practiced nor cultivated at all.
One thousand two hundred and thirty years ago,
in the year Jiaxu of the Zhengyuan era during the reign of Emperor Fei of the Wei dynasty,
the five thousand stanzas were first transmitted.
It was placed in the Guest House of Jiaozhou.
It was brought here during the Western Jin and Yao Qin periods,
as explained in detail in the biographical records.
One should know that, depending on the capacity of the recipient, there is the distinction between the raw and the ripe;
thus, the timing of their concealment or manifestation differs. This is according to the *Niyata-vyākaraṇa* (the teaching on those destined for enlightenment).
When the Buddha, the Bhagavat, entered parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the unsurpassed Dharma to the sixteen great arhats and their retinues.
And he commanded them to protect and uphold it,
so that it would not perish or disappear.
These were the sixteen Arhats.
They shall uphold the True Dharma and bring benefit to sentient beings.
In this region, the lifespan of humans will reach an extreme length of ten years,
during which the Buddha-dharma will temporarily perish and disappear.
Later, when the human lifespan gradually increased to forty thousand years,
Arhats came among humans and clearly expounded the True Dharma.
Thus, for as long as sixty thousand years,
the unsurpassed True Dharma shall circulate in the world,
flourishing and unceasing.
When the human lifespan reaches seventy thousand years,
the unsurpassed True Dharma will have forever vanished;
yet this sutra shall continue to circulate.
It is frequently affected by the Dharma of the Final Age (*mappō*). Throughout the text, it is stated in various places that this occurs during the "Final Age" and the "latter five hundred years.
If one should encounter such a time:
Forgetting both sleep and food, do not let time pass in vain. 3.
The Chronology of Translation. Third: I have carefully examined various catalogs of the scriptures and other sources.
Regarding the dates of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* translations,
there are briefly six periods.
The first is one thousand two hundred and thirty years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
In the first year of the Ganlu era of the Former Wei,
which was the second year of the Wufeng era of the Wu dynasty,
on the seventh day of the seventh month.
The foreigner Zhi Jiangliangjie,
whose name means "Righteousness and Fearlessness," was in the city of Jiaozhou.
It was transcribed by the śramaṇa Daoxin and translated in six fascicles;
this is the one titled the *Fahua Sanmei Jing* (The Scripture on the Samādhi of the Lotus).
The second period was one thousand two hundred and forty years.
In the first year of the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty,
the year of Yibyou (165 CE), the śramaṇa Dharmaruci from the country of Yuezhi [arrived].
His name in the Jin language was Dharmarakṣa;
his secular surname was Zhi.
He traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions.
He understood the languages and scripts of thirty-six countries and brought Sanskrit manuscripts from the kingdom of India;
he translated them into six fascicles.
This is what is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thirdly,
during the reign of Emperor Wu of Jin, in the seventh year of Taikang (the Bingwu year),
he translated it extensively into ten fascicles.
This is what is called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month in the first year of the Yongxi era,
the bhikṣu Kang Na-lü.
When the transcription was completed in Luoyang,
he was accompanied by the upāsakas Zhang Jibo, Dong Jingxuan, Liu Changwu, and Changwen, who were all pure in their observance of the precepts and boundaries,
as they held the manuscript of the scripture in their hands.
He went to the residence of Bai Ma Rong,
where he engaged in oral debate on ancient teachings with Fa Hu.
He expounded the profound meaning.
On the fourteenth day of the ninth month, during the original fasting period,
he held a great dāna assembly at Dongnyu Monastery.
They recited and lectured on this sutra from daybreak until nightfall,
all of whom were filled with joy; having thus completed their task,
they once again collated and finalized the text.
Fourth, in the year 1284 [of the era], the first year of the Xiankang period of the Eastern Jin dynasty, the year Yiwu (1357 CE),
the śramaṇa Zhi Daolin translated it into six fascicles.
This refers to the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of the Lotus. Fifth,
one thousand three hundred and fifty-three years [after the Buddha's passing] corresponds to the seventh year of Hongshi in the Yao Qin dynasty, the Jiachen year.
The Indian śramaṇa Kumārajīva— translated as "Child Longevity" (Tóngshòu) in the Qin language—
was at the Xiāoyáo Garden in Cháng'ān.
It was translated in seven or eight fascicles;
this is what is known as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Kumārajīva and Dharmarakṣa were separated from one another.
Adding one hundred and more years—
specifically fifteen hundred and fifty years—
it corresponds to the first year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, the Xin-you year.
The śramaṇa Guptagupta translated it at Xingshan Temple in seven fascicles;
this is the work known as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra with Added Chapters*.
The preface to the sutra states:
"Upon examining and verifying the two translations by Dharmarakṣa and Kumārajīva,
it is certain that they were not based on a single original text."
